Turf around the pool cage in Davenport's resort homes

Pool-area turf in Davenport uses the residential market range, $8–$18 a square foot installed, typically $10–$16, as of September 2026. In resort subdivisions such as Solterra, where every home is built with its own pool, that turf usually goes inside a screened cage rather than an open yard.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a screened lanai at a resort home

Say you have a 350 sq ft pool deck inside a screen cage at a Solterra-style rental home, with a poured concrete slab already in place around the pool shell. At the typical $10–$16 range, 350 sq ft of turf-over-concrete runs about $3,500 to $5,600 installed, with the drainage underlay and edge-gluing adding labor a bare-soil yard wouldn't need at that same square footage.

Every home with a pool changes what "pool turf" means here

Solterra Resort's homes are built with a private pool as standard rather than an upgrade (Solterra Resort's community profile), and Providence and several neighboring subdivisions follow a similar pattern. That makes pool-cage turf one of the more routine calls in Davenport's newer neighborhoods, rather than a one-off request tied to a single custom home, and it means most of these jobs happen inside a screen enclosure from the start.

Infill choice for turf that sits right at the waterline

Turf bordering a Davenport pool still falls under the same single-family infill rule as the rest of the lot: clean silica sand, zeolite, or a coated sand with a non-toxic coating, never a rubber or synthetic fill outside the footprint of playground equipment. Coated sand is a reasonable pick for a strip that takes regular splash, since the coating resists bacteria growth on the grains themselves rather than relying on the sand alone. Plain silica works fine further back from the coping where splash rarely reaches. Either choice still goes in at roughly one to two pounds per square foot, brushed evenly through the pile.

Turf over concrete inside the cage

A lanai slab poured for a resort-home pool cage needs a drainage underlay and glued-down edges rather than the washed-rock base a lawn gets, since there's no soil underneath to grade or compact. On a Davenport builder home, that slab is usually flat and recently poured, which simplifies the layout compared with an older, settled patio elsewhere in the county.

What actually holds up a turf ribbon between pavers?

A narrow strip of turf set into a paver joint near the pool does not sit on a rock base at all; the pavers themselves carry the load, and the turf gets a thin leveling layer of sand in the joint rather than the two to four inches used everywhere else on a Davenport lot. That thin joint still has to drain rather than trap water against the paver edges, so the sand underneath needs to stay loose enough to percolate, the same principle behind leaving native soil uncompacted under a full-size base. A joint packed too tight holds water at the surface just as a bad rock base would.

What a wall of pool-cage sliders can do to the turf below

Large sliding glass doors are common on Davenport pool homes, and a low-emissivity coating on that much glass can reflect enough concentrated sunlight to soften turf directly in its path, since polyethylene blades start to give around 175 to 200°F under that kind of focused heat. The damage shows up as a scorched patch shaped by the reflection angle rather than by foot traffic, which is often the first clue it is glare and not wear. Checking a west- or south-facing wall of sliders before laying turf close to it avoids relocating a section later.

Confirming the drain point before infill goes down

Once the drainage underlay is glued to a Davenport lanai floor but before any infill goes in, the crew runs water across the surface to confirm it actually reaches the deck's existing drain rather than pooling in a low spot the underlay created by accident. Catching a flat or misdirected section at this stage means lifting a corner of underlay and reworking it, which is straightforward before infill is down and considerably more disruptive after. This check takes a few minutes and is the reason a finished lanai floor rarely surprises anyone with standing water months later.

Keeping the deck drain clear inside a screen enclosure

A screen mesh keeps most large debris out of a Davenport lanai, but pollen, dust, and small leaves still settle on the turf and can work toward the deck drain over time, especially during the June-to-September rainy season when storms are frequent enough that the drain rarely gets a rest. A quick sweep or rinse toward the drain on a regular schedule keeps the whole underlay system doing what it was built for, since even a permeable backing cannot help much once the drain it feeds is the part that is actually clogged.

Guest turnover raises the traffic question

Where a pool-cage home doubles as a short-term rental, which is common in Davenport's resort subdivisions, the turf around the pool sees a new set of feet every few days rather than one family's routine. We spec a denser, better-stabilized product for that traffic pattern, since a lighter economy turf mats faster under back-to-back guest turnovers than it would in an owner-occupied home.

Questions people ask

Does turf over a Davenport lanai slab need a different base than a lawn?

Yes. Concrete gets a drainage underlay and adhesive-secured edges instead of compacted crushed rock, since there's no soil layer to grade underneath the slab.

Do rental-home pool cages need a heavier-duty turf product?

We recommend it. A short-term rental's pool area sees more foot traffic per month than an owner-occupied home, so a denser, better-stabilized product holds its texture longer under that turnover.
